art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. This Saturday's art news runs from your own Grenoble museum, through Lyon and Paris, to openings in London, Washington and Sydney.

Let me begin close to home. At the Musée de Grenoble, there is a show of sculptures and paintings by Anne Truitt. The listing from jds.fr is very short and gives no dates, so I would check the museum's own page before you plan a visit. And today, Saturday the seventh of November, at half past four in the afternoon, the museum offers a guided tour of the François Morellet display, called "Under the geometry, the mischief". Morellet's geometric abstraction is playful, and a guide is a good way into it. If you can get down to the city this afternoon, that could be a pleasant hour.

Two other regional stories caught my eye. Lyon Capitale reports eight poetry evenings, "listening to our planet", at the Musée de la Résistance et de la Déportation in Isère. The dates weren't given in the piece, but poetry in that setting sounds well worth following up. And in the Drôme, ici.fr tells us that shoes from the Musée de la chaussure in Romans are taking up residence at the château de Grignan. The article explains why, though I only have the headline, so I can't say more. Still, it's a charming pairing of a museum collection with a historic château.

Now to Lyon, where history comes through images and storytelling. Le Petit Bulletin Grenoble writes about a comic book on the women drivers, nurses and rescuers of military emergency units. It is linked to an exhibition at the CHRD and centres on the military doctor Madeleine Pauliac. The comic's creators describe it as telling "a blind spot of history", and I like the idea of a graphic narrative recovering a chapter that was neglected for so long. Also in Lyon, since the second of November, there are two exhibitions of Blaise Adilon's photography, at Le Bleu du Ciel and at the maison Georges Adilon, along with a new monograph. The work asks how one might provoke the real into producing another image, which is a rather beautiful way to put it.

Turning to art and literature, which I know is closest to your heart. In Paris, the BnF is staging an exhibition on the obsessions of Georges Perec. Beaux Arts Magazine calls it abundant, and it draws on more than forty years of his work across literature and the visual arts. Given how much Perec played with lists, spaces and images, it seems the right writer for a show that joins words and pictures.

Then there is a painting with a heartbreaking story. In Hyperallergic, Catherine Ostler follows the two girls in Renoir's "Pink and Blue". They grew up in a privileged, elite artistic French family, and their lives were overturned by the Holocaust. It's a story in which a bright, affectionate portrait opens onto a darker history, and I suspect it might make a good starting point for a conversation with older pupils about how paintings carry what happened to the people in them.

And a piece of good news for book lovers. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that an anonymous benefactor has apparently rescued the cabinet des livres at the Château de Chantilly, which holds about thirteen thousand precious volumes. The text I have is cut short, so the details are thin, but the outcome is heartening: a library saved for future readers.

Next, two stories about how we look at paintings, and who they belong to. At the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, a pop-up restoration studio will let visitors watch live conservation of a seventeenth-century group portrait by Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy, showing an Amsterdam wine guild. Hyperallergic reports it as a rare chance to see how a painting is actually brought back to life. And in London, the National Gallery has released a video about NG Citizens, an assembly of fifty people chosen by lottery to consider how the Gallery should connect people and paintings. The question underneath it is a thoughtful one: what should a national collection mean to the people it belongs to?

Finally, a round of international openings, mostly from The Guardian. At the V&A in South Kensington, from today until the ninth of May, an exhibition traces the story of one city, following Ottoman court tulips and silks back to the palace of Emperor Constantine. It's history told through objects, and the layers sound fascinating. In Washington, the National Gallery of Art opens "Remember Me" today, running until the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. It brings together seventy works showing how African Americans used portrait photography to picture themselves and their communities, with themes of identity, resilience and community. Those are images that carry history in their faces.

In Sydney, Powerhouse Parramatta, a new museum costing nine hundred and fifteen million Australian dollars, opens this weekend in the city's west, with five exhibitions and a twenty-three-day festival. The Guardian also looks at the building's contested history, which gives useful context to this major new cultural space.

And to end on something lively, The Guardian talks to Emma Richardson, bass player with the Pixies, about her large, vivid oil paintings as her show "Hotwire My Heart" opens. The paintings seem to swing between explosion and implosion, and it sounds like a very painterly read about a life spent crossing between music and art.

That's all for today, Yamuna. I hope Morellet's mischief makes your afternoon a good one.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the seventh of November, and today's art news has a pleasing thread running through it: pictures that carry stories, from a Renoir with a painful sequel to a library saved by a stranger, with a few good things happening close to home.

Let me start in Grenoble, because there is something on today. The Musée de Grenoble is offering a guided tour of its François Morellet display, called "Under the geometry, the mischief", this afternoon at half past four. Morellet is a lovely artist to be guided through, because his geometric abstraction is playful. The title itself promises that beneath the grids and lines there is a sense of humour waiting to be found. If you fancy an unhurried Saturday afternoon among clever, cheerful shapes, this is the one. The tour is listed for today only, so it's one to decide on over breakfast.

The same museum is also showing sculptures and paintings by Anne Truitt. I should be honest that the listing from the Journal des Sports is very short. It gives no dates and no further detail, so I can't tell you how long the show runs or what exactly is on the walls. But since it is at the Musée de Grenoble itself, it seems worth a quick look at the museum's own pages before you plan a visit, and perhaps pairing it with the Morellet tour if the timing works.

Still within the Isère, there is something that should speak to the poet in you. Lyon Capitale reports on eight poetry evenings, titled "listening to our planet", at the Musée de la Résistance et de la Déportation. The report as I have it doesn't give the dates, so you will need to check with the museum. But the combination appeals: poetry spoken in a place devoted to memory, with the natural world as the theme. It is a setting where words are likely to carry real weight.

And a little further afield, in the Drôme, there is a charming curiosity. According to ici.fr, shoes from the Musée de la chaussure in Romans are taking up residence at the château de Grignan. The article explains why, but all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you the reason. What I can say is that it pairs a humble, intimate object with a grand historic house, and a pair of shoes can tell you a great deal about the person who wore them. You will know better than most how much a novelist can do with a detail like that.

Now to Lyon, where two stories look at how images and history meet. The first is from Le Petit Bulletin, which writes about a comic book on a part of history that has been largely overlooked: the women drivers, nurses and rescuers who served in military emergency units. The book is linked to an exhibition at the CHRD, the Lyon history centre devoted to the Resistance and the Deportation, and it is centred on a military doctor, Madeleine Pauliac. The journalist's phrase, as quoted, is that "we are telling a blind spot of history". I like that idea: a graphic narrative bringing a neglected chapter into the light, much as a good novel can. It might even make a fine example for a class on how stories recover voices that official accounts left out.

The second Lyon story is about photography. Since the second of November, there have been two exhibitions of Blaise Adilon's work, one at Le Bleu du Ciel and one at the maison Georges Adilon, along with a new monograph. Le Petit Bulletin describes the work as asking how to provoke the real into producing another image. That is a rather lovely way to put it. It suggests photographs that don't simply record the world but coax something second and stranger out of it, which is not far from what a poet does with a plain sentence.

That leads me neatly to the links between art and literature, which I know are close to your heart. At the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, Beaux Arts Magazine describes a sprawling exhibition devoted to the obsessions of Georges Perec. It draws on more than forty years of his work, across literature and the visual arts, and the magazine calls it foisonnante, which means teeming or abundant. Perec's writing and the images around it are meant to be read together, so the show seems to treat that link as the very point. From the little I have, it sounds like the sort of exhibition where a reader could happily lose an entire afternoon, following one fixation from page to picture and back again.

From Paris to a painting with a story attached. In Hyperallergic, Catherine Ostler follows the two girls in Renoir's "Pink and Blue". They grew up with a privileged life in an elite artistic French family, and that life was overturned by the Holocaust. The painting, which on its surface is a gentle double portrait of two sisters, becomes the doorway into a history of family, art and persecution. It is exactly the sort of piece where a canvas teaches history in the way a good novel does, through particular people rather than dates. If you are ever looking for a way to bring the period into a classroom through an image, this could be a quietly powerful starting point.

And there is some heartening news for book lovers. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that an anonymous benefactor has reportedly rescued the cabinet des livres at the Château de Chantilly. That is the book cabinet, home to about thirteen thousand precious volumes. The text I have is cut short, so I can't give you the details of the rescue or what was at risk. But the headline is the good part: a mysterious donor, a historic library, and thirteen thousand books preserved for readers still to come. It has something of a storybook feel, with a secret patron stepping in at the right moment.

Two exhibitions that opened yesterday, on opposite sides of the world, both use objects to tell the story of people and places. In Washington, the National Gallery of Art has opened "Remember Me", which runs until the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. The Guardian presents it in pictures. It brings together seventy works showing how African Americans used portrait photography to picture themselves and their communities, and the themes it names are identity, resilience and community. Early portrait photography could be a means of dignity and self-definition, and these images carry that history on their faces. They may be a good reminder that a portrait can be an act of authorship as much as a painted or written one.

In London, the Victoria and Albert Museum in South Kensington has an exhibition that runs from the seventh of November until the ninth of May. The Guardian, in its week-in-art column, describes it as tracing a story from Ottoman court tulips and silks back to the palace of Emperor Constantine. It is the layered history of a single city told through its beautiful things, and the idea of following a tulip pattern back through centuries to an emperor's palace has a real narrative pull. It sounds as if the show wants you to read objects as chapters.

Another group of stories this morning is about how museums open themselves up, and who they are for. In Boston, the Museum of Fine Arts is going to set up a pop-up restoration studio, so that visitors can watch live conservation of a seventeenth-century group portrait by Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy. The painting shows an Amsterdam wine guild. Hyperallergic points out how rare it is to see how a painting is actually brought back to life, and I rather like the idea of standing before a Dutch group portrait while someone patiently works on it a few feet away. It turns a finished masterpiece into something still unfolding.

In London, the National Gallery has released a video about a project called NG Citizens. This is a citizens' assembly of fifty people, chosen by lottery, who are considering how the Gallery should connect people and paintings. The video asks what the National Gallery should mean to the people it belongs to. It is a thoughtful question, and one that applies well beyond London: who is a national collection for, and what should it offer them? I would be curious to hear what answers a group of ordinary visitors comes up with.

And in Sydney, the Guardian reports that Powerhouse Parramatta opens this weekend. It is a new museum in western Sydney, costing nine hundred and fifteen million Australian dollars, opening with five exhibitions and a twenty-three-day festival. The Guardian calls it dazzling inside and out, and the article also covers the building's contested history, which gives useful context to a major new cultural space. It is a reminder that a museum's walls have their own stories, and that not everyone agrees on how they should be told.

Finally, something painterly and lively to end on. The Guardian profiles Emma Richardson, the Pixies' bass player, whose show "Hotwire My Heart" is opening. She talks about her large, vivid oil paintings, and the headline asks, with a certain relish, whether one of them is an explosion, an implosion or something else entirely. The piece sounds like a lively read about a creative life that moves between music and painting, and about how big, bold colour can leave a viewer unsure what they are looking at, which is often the best sign that a picture is working.

So that is the morning's art news, Yamuna: enjoy the Morellet tour if you go, and may the rest of your Saturday be as full of good stories as these.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich day for readers, with the Booker shortlist still drawing a lot of attention, a good few pieces on art and writing, and some lovely lyrical language to finish on.

Let me begin with the Booker, since three critics have now weighed in. The i Paper has a reviewer who says they have read every novel on this year's shortlist and argues there is a clear winner. I'd love to tell you which, but the piece is the place for that, and it's a pleasure to follow someone making a case after reading the whole list. The Irish Times takes a different route. Its critic has also read the shortlist and finds two novels that are brilliant at capturing what it is like to live through the mess of the twenties. So if you are building a reading list, that is a useful pointer to where to start.

The Guardian, meanwhile, asks this year's finalists, including Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout, where their novels began. The teaser promises a trip to the Scottish islands, a psychological experiment and a chance encounter in a drugstore. Writers tend to be at their most vivid when they describe the first spark, so it should be good listening for a teacher who likes to show pupils how a story begins.

The Booker Prizes site itself offers two pieces. One is an extract from Max Porter's Lanny, a direct taste of that novel's voice and language, and well worth reading aloud. The other is a list of eight Booker books inspired by folklore, which links prize-winning fiction to myth and older traditions of storytelling. And on a related note, Firstpost has a Gen Z reader revisiting Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things, a Booker winner, with a very sharp take. It's a nice reminder of how a novel with such a distinctive narrative voice and lyrical prose can feel new to a younger reader, and perhaps a thought for your own pupils.

Now to the meeting of art and words. This year marks the centenary of John Berger, and The Guardian has a "where to start" guide to his work, which crosses genres and takes in art, love and mortality. Given how his writing on painting and on seeing has shaped so many readers, it's a lovely way to approach him, or return to him. Literary Hub has Priyanka Kumar on bringing art into her nature writing, drawing on a snowy encounter with a coyote near her home and on her idea of the microwild. It's a thoughtful piece about how looking closely at pictures can change the way we write about place. And in The Guardian's poetry roundup, Jessica Mookherjee's collection The Universe Is an Animal mixes scientific language with family histories of partition and displacement. One poem reworks Monet's waterlilies into something darker, which I thought you might enjoy, given your fondness for those crossings between canvas and page.

On poetry and the sound of language, Literary Hub prints Mahmoud Darwish's poem "Arabic Music" in full. It is meditative, full of questions about stones, clouds and sparrows, and it asks to be read slowly and aloud. Literary Hub also has an excerpt from a story called "Dams", in which a character named Ada, over coffee, explains why she has come back, and notices the translucence of the words escriure and novel·la. It's a small, attentive moment about how words look and feel, and it suits a literary reader very well. Also in The Guardian, the Indian-Irish poet Nikita Gill talks about her early reading. She remembers being at sea with her sailor father, and a retelling of the Mahabharata that inspired her to write. She admires Arundhati Roy and Lucille Clifton, and says she read Flowers in the Attic too young, and that someone should have stopped her. It's a warm, personal interview about how a poet is made by what she reads.

Lastly, a few pieces about place and the ordinary. The American Library in Paris has named the winner of its 2026 Book Award, which honours fiction and nonfiction that draw on France as a timeless source of inspiration. The winner is Hotel Exile: Paris, a title that will probably appeal to anyone who loves the city and the way it sits in writing. The Guardian reviews Paul Theroux's True North, in which the veteran travel writer turns his observant eye on Canada and its people. The review opens with a sharp border-crossing episode that sets the tone for his wry, detailed style. And Literary Hub asks who gets to write about ordinary life, in an essay on Sergey Davydov's novel Мидвест, his prose work outside the theatre. It argues that his story of ordinary life is really a love story, and that readers should accept his way of telling it.

That's the round-up for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it makes its way onto your bedside table.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich day for the Literature briefing, with the Booker shortlist still the main talking point, plenty of poetry, and a good deal of writing about how words and pictures meet.

Let me begin with the Booker, because several pieces have appeared at once, and together they make a rather good reading group. The i Paper has a reviewer who says they have read every novel on this year's shortlist, and who argues there is a clear winner. I like a critic who commits. It's one thing to admire a single book from a shortlist; it's another to have lived with all of them and then say, plainly, this one. I won't spoil the verdict, partly because I'd rather you read the argument than receive the answer, and partly because the interest is in how the case is made.

The Irish Times takes a slightly different route. Its critic has also read the 2026 shortlist and finds two novels that are brilliant on what it is to live through the mess of the 2020s. That phrase, the mess of the 2020s, is a good one, and it raises a question you may recognise from the classroom: what do we ask of a novel written in the middle of its own moment? Do we want it to explain the disorder, or simply to stay inside it with us, with a convincing voice? The Irish Times suggests that two of these books manage the second, and do it very well. It's a useful piece if you're building a reading list, since it points you towards where the critic thinks the strongest writing lies.

Then The Guardian has a lovely idea. It has asked this year's Booker finalists, among them Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout, to describe where their novels began. The piece is called Narrative threads, and the teaser hints at wonderfully varied beginnings: a trip to the Scottish islands, a psychological experiment, and a chance encounter in a drugstore. I find these origin stories fascinating, because they remind us that a finished novel, with all its architecture, usually starts as something small and slightly accidental. A place, an odd idea, a stranger glimpsed for a moment. If your older pupils ever feel that writing begins with some grand plan, this might be a gentle corrective. A drugstore encounter can turn into a book.

For a direct taste of prose, The Booker Prizes site offers an extract from Max Porter's Lanny. I haven't got more to tell you about the passage itself, but what the site is offering is the voice and the language, and that's exactly what Porter is known for in readers' minds: writing that you want to hear rather than merely read. It might be a good one to read aloud, either to yourself on a quiet evening or, with some careful selection, to a class.

The same site has a list of eight Booker Prizes books inspired by folklore. This links nicely with something you value, the novel as a vehicle for older storytelling, where myth and tradition carry history in ways that a textbook can't. A list like this is a good way into thinking about how contemporary fiction borrows from, and argues with, the stories that came before it. And it sits well beside another piece from Firstpost, in which a Gen Z reader revisits Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things, a Booker winner, and gives it what the headline calls a very sharp take. I find this kind of piece rather heartening. Here is a novel with a strong narrative voice and richly lyrical prose, and a younger reader coming to it fresh, and responding to it directly rather than reverently. If you have première pupils who are wary of anything labelled a classic, it might be worth seeing how this reviewer approaches it. Roy turns up elsewhere in today's reading too, but I'll come to that.

Now to poetry, which has been well served. The Guardian's interview with the Indian-Irish poet Nikita Gill is, I think, the most personal piece of the day. Its title is a quotation: I read Flowers in the Attic too young, someone should have stopped me. She talks about her earliest reading memories, which took place at sea, travelling with her father, who was a sailor. There's something quite moving in the image of a child reading while the ocean moves beneath her. She also talks about a retelling of the Mahabharata that inspired her to start writing, and she names her admiration for Arundhati Roy and for Lucille Clifton. It's an interview about the making of a poet, and it's really an interview about reading: how what we devour as children, sometimes unsuitably, ends up shaping what we later make. It might even prompt a good conversation with your seconde pupils about the books they read too early, or the ones that first made them want to write.

Literary Hub, meanwhile, prints in full Mahmoud Darwish's poem Arabic Music. It is built on meditative questions, about stones, clouds and sparrows, and it has exactly the quality you enjoy in poetry: it is musical, patient, and made for the voice. There's a gentle rhythm to a poem that asks questions rather than making statements. The questions seem to open space around them, and the stones and clouds and sparrows become something like instruments in the music of the title. It is the kind of poem to read slowly and then again, aloud, and I'd suggest it's worth setting aside a few minutes for it today.

The Guardian's roundup of recent poetry adds a third voice. It includes Jessica Mookherjee's collection The Universe Is an Animal, which mixes scientific language with family histories of partition and displacement. I find that combination striking: the vocabulary of science, which tends to sound cool and impersonal, set against stories of people uprooted and separated. The roundup also mentions a poem that reworks Monet's waterlilies into something darker. That one will interest you particularly, given your love of the links between paintings and written work. Monet's waterlilies are usually a byword for calm and shimmering light, so to turn them dark is a bold act of reading, a kind of argument with the painting. If you were ever to teach ekphrastic poetry, a poem like this could make an excellent contrast with more reverent responses to art.

Which brings me neatly to the pieces that connect writing with the visual world. This week marks the centenary of John Berger, and The Guardian has published a where-to-start guide to his work. Berger is hard to pin down: he wrote about art, love, mortality and much else, and he moved between forms in a way that resists a single label. The guide is meant for newcomers, and it seems a gentle map for a writer who doesn't offer an obvious front door. Since Berger's essays on painting and on seeing sit right at the meeting-point of your interests, it may be the most natural item of the day for you. Even if you know him already, a centenary is a good moment to return.

On Literary Hub, Priyanka Kumar writes about incorporating art into her nature writing. She draws on a snowy encounter with a coyote near her home, and on her concept of what she calls the microwild. I find the idea appealing: that wildness isn't only found in remote landscapes, but in small encounters close to where we live. And I wonder whether you, up in Les Adrets with Belledonne behind you, might recognise something of it, the way a creature crossing the snow near the house can rearrange an ordinary day. The piece is about how looking at paintings, and thinking about how artists see, can sharpen the way a writer sees a place. It's a thoughtful essay about attention.

Attention is also what animates two pieces of fiction and criticism from Literary Hub. The first is an excerpt from a story called Dams, in which a woman named Ada, over coffee, explains why she has come back. As she does so, she notices the translucence of two words, escriure and novel·la, to write and novel. What I love about that detail is that the scene turns a plain conversation into an act of listening to language itself. She isn't just explaining her return, she is looking through the words as though they were glass. It's attentive, lyrical prose, the sort that rewards slow reading, and it might be a lovely example for pupils of how a narrator's close attention to words can reveal character.

The second is an essay with a good title, Who Gets to Write About Ordinary Life? It concerns Sergey Davydov's novel, whose Russian title reads Midwest, and which is his prose work outside the theatre. The essay argues that his story of ordinary life is really a love story, and that readers should accept his way of telling it. I like the generosity of that last point. It asks us to meet a book on its own terms rather than measuring it against what we expected. And the question in the title is a useful one for any literature teacher: whose everyday lives become the subject of serious fiction, and why do we sometimes assume that the ordinary is less worthy of a novel than the extraordinary?

Finally, two pieces about place and travel. The American Library in Paris has named the winner of its 2026 Book Award, which honours fiction and nonfiction that draw on France as a timeless source of inspiration. The winner is Hotel Exile: Paris. I'm only able to tell you the title, but it's a good one: it holds together the idea of a hotel, a temporary shelter, with exile, and sets both in a city that has long been a refuge for writers. Given your fondness for Paris and for the way places shape writing, it's one to note down.

And The Guardian reviews True North, Paul Theroux's travel book about Canada, which it describes as an American's view of the country. The review opens with a sharp border-crossing episode that sets the tone for his wry, detailed travel writing. Theroux is a veteran, and the review suggests he turns the same observant eye on Canada and its people that readers know from his earlier journeys. Border crossings are a wonderful way into a travel book, since they are a moment when a writer is looked at as much as looking, and I suspect this review will tempt you towards the book itself.

So that's the day: a shortlist being argued over, poets remembering how they began to read, a painter's waterlilies turned dark, and a woman looking through a word as though through glass. I hope one of them keeps you company with your coffee this morning.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the seventh of November, and this week's news from around Les Adrets has a gentle cultural leaning, with a few things happening today and several others worth pencilling in for the weeks ahead.

Let's start with today, because there are three things close to home. This evening, from half past six until ten o'clock, the village hall at Saint-Jean-le-Vieux hosts an evening of Belledonne-themed storytelling and gatherings. The listing is short on detail, but the idea of voices telling tales of the mountain on a November night seems made for you. Earlier in the day, from ten until one o'clock, three artists are meeting visitors at the library in La Combe-de-Lancey. The listing doesn't say what kind of art they make, so it's a bit of a surprise, but a morning of conversation with working artists in a small village library has its own charm. And in Grenoble, a month-long photography programme begins today and runs until the twenty-ninth of November. It's listed as free, though the listing names neither venues nor photographers, so do take it as a lead to check rather than a firm plan. Mesinfos also has a roundup of things to do in Grenoble this weekend, through to Sunday, though without details of the individual events.

Yesterday evening was a busy one in the valley, if you happened to be out. In Pontcharra, the Muchmuche Company performed AMOURS, as part of the Saison Echos season. And at the Dupanloup village hall in La Combe-de-Lancey, the Péninsule Trio gave a concert. Neither listing says much about the form or the programme, but I mention them because both are part of a steady rhythm of live performance in the Grésivaudan, and the Saison Echos in particular may be worth keeping an eye on for coming weeks.

Looking ahead to music and performance, there are three leads. The first is a baroque concert in Eybens, near Grenoble, called Venice at the Time of Vivaldi, reported by the Journal des Sports... or rather, by jds dot f r, which doesn't give a date, so you'll want to look that up. Given your love of classical music, it seems worth the search. The second concerns the singer Raphaël, who is playing at the MC2 in Grenoble. Le Dauphiné Libéré is offering readers the chance to meet him beforehand, but the date isn't in the listing, so check with the venue. The third is further off and quite different. On the third of December at six in the evening, the Théâtre Hexagone in Meylan presents Hypertemps, by Clément Edouard. It's a one-hour sound installation and performance exploring time, rhythm and listening, and there are three further dates if that evening doesn't suit. It sounds like a piece for someone who listens closely to the shape and music of language, so it may well appeal.

Over in Chambéry, Le Dauphiné Libéré has two stories that are rather lovely in different ways. The first is about volunteers who are restoring old trains and getting them back onto the rails. It's a warm heritage story, with a clear sense of people giving their time to something worthwhile. The second is about an exhibition that aims to demystify the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela. The report is brief, so I can't tell you more about its content, but the Camino has such a long history and such a rich literary tradition that a local exhibition on it feels like a natural thing for you to look into.

For something a little different, there's a guided visit of the Champiloop mushroom farm in Saint-Martin-d'Hères, in the Grenoble metropolis. Again, jds dot f r doesn't give a date, but it's a pleasantly curious sort of outing, part craft, part food, and the sort of thing that might end with a basket of something interesting for supper.

And now a few things for the coming months, for when the diary needs filling. In Villard-Bonnot, the Printemps des arts, the spring arts festival, is already being prepared for 2027, and registrations are due to open soon. Le Dauphiné Libéré's report is short, but it's one to watch if you like local culture in the spring. In Meylan, the Scène nationale Hexagone has announced the thirteenth edition of the EXPERIMENTA biennial, due in 2027. No dates are fixed yet, but it promises eighty proposals of exhibitions, shows and performances, drawn from twenty-three partners across the territory. That's a great deal of material for anyone who likes paintings and performance meeting one another.

Finally, a practical note for winter. Les 7 Laux, which takes in Prapoutel, Le Pleynet and Pipay, has announced its season: it opens on the nineteenth of December and runs until the twenty-ninth of March, 2027. There will be a hundred and twenty kilometres of pistes, a snowpark and a luge on rails, all about forty minutes from both Grenoble and Chambéry. Even if skiing isn't your priority, it's good to know that the season's dates are settled if you fancy planning winter weekends close to home.

So, a storytelling evening tonight and a long list of things to look forward to; I hope some of it finds its way into your weekend.
around.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the seventh of November, and the last two days have turned up a pleasant mix of village evenings, music, small exhibitions and a few things to put in the diary for the colder months.

Let me begin with today, because there are three things happening close to home, and one of them suits you particularly well.

This evening, from half past six until ten o'clock, the village hall at Saint-Jean-le-Vieux hosts an evening of storytelling and gatherings on the theme of Belledonne. The listing comes from the Grésivaudan agenda, and it describes the sort of event the mountains do rather well: people coming together in a hall in the dark of early November, and the old habit of the veillée, the evening spent sitting and listening. I can't tell you who is telling the stories or what they are, because the listing doesn't say. But for someone who loves a good narrator, and who lives on the slopes of the very range being celebrated, it's a natural fit and very close to your door. If you fancy going, it's worth finding out whether the evening is drop-in or whether you need to book, since the listing doesn't mention it.

Earlier today, from ten until one, the library at La Combe-de-Lancey welcomes three artists who are there to meet visitors. The agenda doesn't say what kind of art they make, whether painting, drawing, sculpture or something else, so I won't guess. But a morning of conversation with working artists, in a small village library, has a certain appeal. Libraries are good places for that sort of exchange, because the books are right there, and the talk can wander easily between images and words. It finishes at one o'clock, so if you're reading or listening to this late, you may have only a little of it left.

Also beginning today in Grenoble is Le mois de la photo, a month of photography running from today until the twenty-ninth of November. It's listed as free. I should be honest that the listing gives no venues and no names of photographers, so think of it as a lead to follow up rather than a firm plan. Still, a month-long programme, with free entry, leaves you plenty of room to choose a quiet afternoon. And photography, of course, sits close to what you love about the links between paintings and written work: how an image can be read like a paragraph, how a single frame can hold a whole narrative. If you do find a venue worth visiting, a series of portraits or landscapes might make a lovely thing to show a class one day.

For the weekend in Grenoble more broadly, the site mesinfos has published a roundup of things to do from Friday the sixth to Sunday the eighth of November. The text I have doesn't give details of the individual events, so I can't pick out highlights for you. But if you are heading into the city tomorrow, it's a handy place to look for a gap in the Sunday plans.

Now, a word about yesterday evening, Friday the sixth, in the Grésivaudan. Two events took place, and I mention them partly in case you went, and partly because they show how lively the valley's programme is at this time of year. In Pontcharra there was a performance called AMOURS, by Cie Muchmuche Company, part of the Saison Echos season. The listing doesn't describe the form or the content, so I can't say whether it was dance, theatre or something in between. And at the Dupanloup village hall in La Combe-de-Lancey, the Péninsule Trio gave a concert. The programme and genre aren't stated. Both have passed, but the Saison Echos name is worth remembering. If AMOURS caught your eye, it suggests that the season has more to offer through the winter, and the Grésivaudan agenda is the place to watch for it.

Turning to music, which I know is close to your heart, there are two items that look ahead. In Eybens, just south-east of Grenoble, there is a baroque concert called Venice at the Time of Vivaldi, reported by jds.fr. The date isn't given in the listing, so you will need to check it, but the title alone is promising. Venice in Vivaldi's time was a city of canals, theatres, convents with famous musicians, and carnival masks, and it has fed the imagination of novelists for centuries. A programme drawing on that world would offer plenty to the ear and plenty to the mind, whether or not you know the music well.

And in Grenoble, Le Dauphiné Libéré is offering readers the chance to meet the singer Raphaël before his concert at the MC2. That's in its Face aux lecteurs series. The date of the concert isn't given in the listing, so it would be wise to look at the MC2's own programme for timing. It's a fairly niche item, and not necessarily your first choice of music, but the format, a conversation with an artist before the show, is rather nice, and it reminds you how much of the city's cultural life is about meeting the people behind the work.

A further music-adjacent date for the diary comes from Meylan. On the third of December, at six in the evening, the Théâtre Hexagone presents Hypertemps, a one-hour sound installation and performance by Clément Edouard. It explores time, rhythm and listening, and there are three further dates beyond the third, though I don't have them. What I like about this one for you is the emphasis on listening and on form. You spend your working life teaching pupils to attend closely to how a sentence moves, how rhythm and sound carry meaning, and this sounds like an hour devoted to exactly that kind of attention, only in sound rather than on the page. It might be a good one to book early, given it's a Thursday evening in the run-up to Christmas, and given the Hexagone is a Scène nationale with a loyal audience.

Staying with Meylan, the Hexagone has also announced that the thirteenth edition of the EXPERIMENTA biennial, linked with PERFORMA, is due in 2027. No dates are given yet. What we do know is its scale: eighty proposals of exhibitions, shows and performances, put together by twenty-three partners across the territory. That is a big, spread-out festival, the kind where you can follow your own thread, picking an exhibition here and a performance there. It's too early to plan, but it is a good thing to know is coming, and the dates should follow in due course.

Not far from there, in Villard-Bonnot, preparations are under way for the Printemps des arts 2027, a spring arts festival. Registrations are due to open soon, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. The text is brief, so I can't say whether the registrations are for exhibitors, performers or visitors. But if you've ever wanted to see how a local arts festival gets organised, or even to take part, this is the moment when the doors begin to open.

Over in Chambéry, Le Dauphiné Libéré has two pieces that I found rather appealing, and both are about people and what they care for.

The first is about volunteers who are restoring old trains and putting them back on the rails. It's a heritage story, but really it's a story about patience and about people giving their time to something they love. There is something very literary about railways, isn't there? So many novels have a train in them, whether it's a journey, a departure, a meeting or an escape, and for generations they were the way stories moved across Europe. Knowing that there are people in Chambéry quietly bringing old rolling stock back to life is a small piece of good news, and the kind that makes a place feel looked after.

The second is an exhibition in Chambéry that aims to demystify the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela. The text I have is short, so I can't tell you where it is on, how long it runs or what's in it. But the Camino is a rich subject. It has a long tradition in writing, from medieval accounts to modern travel books and memoirs, and it's often romanticised. An exhibition that sets out to take some of the myth away, and look at the pilgrimage more plainly, could be quite thought-provoking. It might even sit well beside a class discussion about how a journey is turned into a story, and who gets to tell it. Do check the details before making the trip.

For something a little different, jds.fr reports on a guided visit of the Champiloop mushroom farm in Saint-Martin-d'Hères, in the Grenoble metropolis. The date isn't given, so you'd need to enquire. It's a local craft-and-food outing, the sort of thing that suits a curious person with an appetite. Mushrooms in autumn have a certain charm anyway, and a visit might pair well with a stop at a producers' market afterwards, though that's my suggestion rather than anything in the listing.

Finally, a look ahead to the winter. Les 7 Laux, which takes in Prapoutel, Le Pleynet and Pipay, has announced its ski season: it runs from the nineteenth of December 2026 until the twenty-ninth of March 2027. The resort offers one hundred and twenty kilometres of pistes, a snowpark, and luge on rails, and it is about forty minutes from both Grenoble and Chambéry. For you, living in Les Adrets, it's practically a neighbour, and a useful thing to know if you want to plan winter weekends close to home. The opening is a couple of weeks after the Hypertemps evening in Meylan, so December has some shape to it already.

To gather the practical threads together: today there's the storytelling evening in Saint-Jean-le-Vieux from half past six, the artists' morning at La Combe-de-Lancey library which closes at one, and the start of the photography month in Grenoble. Several other items, the Vivaldi concert in Eybens, the Raphaël concert at the MC2, the Champiloop visit and the Chambéry exhibition, need a quick check of dates before you commit. And further off, the third of December in Meylan, the opening of the ski season on the nineteenth, and the two festivals of 2027 are all worth pencilling in.

That's the round-up for now, Yamuna, and I hope the Belledonne stories tonight keep you warm on the way home.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the BFI corner, with some welcome company from Twelfth Night, Austen and a little music on the side.

Let's begin with Hamlet, since it's on the 2027 list and the stage is full of it. The Guardian has a review of a new production whose headline says it turns Shakespeare inside out with infinite jest, and cuddly toys. The Observer, meanwhile, reviews Lost Dog's The Last Hamlet, praising its shambolic charm and, again, its soft toys. The two headlines sound very alike, though the snippets I have don't confirm they are the same show, so do check before you quote either. Either way, the idea is a delightful one for a classroom. A Hamlet played with soft toys invites a good question for première: what happens to grief, madness and revenge when the staging turns playful? You could ask students whether the comedy undermines the tragedy or reveals something in it. Yorick's skull and that "infinite jest" line seem a natural doorway into the discussion.

On screen, The Hindu reviews a new Hamlet film starring Riz Ahmed, and its headline says he finds method in this madness. That's a neat play on Polonius's famous remark about Hamlet's behaviour, and it might be a fun starting point for a lesson on whether Hamlet's madness is real or performed. I only have the headline and a short summary, so I can't say more about the film itself.

Two more items are really just doorways. The University of Utah has a piece titled "Why Hamlet still matters", which could offer framing for a seconde class meeting the play for the first time, although I only have the title. And Starburst Magazine interviews Dan Sturman and R.C. Staab about Space Hamlet, a science-fiction reworking of the play. The extract is thin, but the idea of Hamlet in space is a good prompt for asking what survives when you strip away Elsinore: the ghost, the delay, the doubt. Finally, BroadwayWorld has a video preview of Hamlet at the Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey. It's only a caption, but a preview clip is just the sort of thing you can play for five minutes and then ask students how they would stage the same scene.

Staying with the stage, there are a few other set texts out in the world. Shakespeare's Globe has an official trailer for its Twelfth Night, which could be a lovely taster for students beginning the play. No other details came with it, but a trailer is short enough to use as a warm-up: what tone does it promise, and does it feel like comedy or melancholy? Also from BroadwayWorld, Ellyn Heald's Twelfth Night: 1941 will have its world premiere at the Episcopal Actors' Guild in New York. The notice gives no date, so only the place is certain, but the title suggests an interesting question about what happens when the play is moved into a particular historical moment. Closer to the heart of Friel's play, the Mount Temple Drama Group in Westmeath, Ireland, is staging Dancing at Lughnasa. It's a brief item and it's a local group, not a professional company, but it's a reminder that Friel's five sisters and their kitchen are still being brought to life in Irish communities.

Moving to the oral themes, there's a charming item for Emma. The Irish Times reviews Catherine Cliff's debut, Miss Bates: Emma Revisited, which retells Austen's novel from the point of view of the gossipy, overlooked Miss Bates. The reviewer calls it witty and ambitious. As a teaching idea, it's rather appealing: Miss Bates is the character Emma humiliates at Box Hill, so hearing the story from her side could open a conversation about narrative perspective and who gets to be the centre of a novel. It's a good exercise for students, too: rewrite a scene from a minor character's viewpoint.

The Financial Times has an essay titled "Cormac McCarthy: A Legacy Revisited", about how his reputation became a myth. The extract I have is thin, but it bears on The Road, and it might help you frame a conversation about how an author's mystique shapes the way we read a book. Then there's Margaret Atwood, who appears twice. The Toronto Star reports that she has thousands of microplastics in her blood and is not happy about it. All I have is the headline, so I can't say more, but it is a reminder of how Atwood's real-world concerns keep brushing against the speculative worlds she writes. And the Miami Book Fair returns from the fifteenth to the twenty-second of November, with a line-up that includes Atwood, Colson Whitehead, Tony Shalhoub and Bonnie Garmus. It's a festival announcement, so mostly useful as a note of where authors are speaking, and perhaps a hint that interviews or recordings may appear in the following days.

Finally, two items for the music lover in you, though neither is directly on the syllabus. AnOther Magazine has an Obsessions Index feature with the composer Max Richter. I only have the title, so I can't tell you what he's obsessed with, but it may well be worth a look. And Bloomberg reports that one of classical music's biggest stars says AI is degrading our taste. The text is brief and I don't have a name, but the question is a good one for a culture teacher: what do we lose when machines can imitate beauty, and how would we explain why a human voice or a written sentence matters?

That's the corner for today. May your Saturday include a good coffee and at least one jest that isn't infinite.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Saturday-morning sort of briefing: a great deal of Hamlet in the news, a little Twelfth Night and Friel, a clever novel about Emma, and a few authors and musicians worth a glance.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since it dominates the last two days, and it's a text on your 2027 list. Two British reviews have appeared, and I suspect they describe the same show, though the summaries I have don't say so. The Guardian carries a review headlined as an extraordinary new Hamlet that turns Shakespeare inside out with infinite jest and cuddly toys. The Observer, meanwhile, reviews a production called The Last Hamlet, by a company named Lost Dog, and describes it as Shakespeare with soft toys and shambolic charm. Two papers, two mentions of soft toys. It's worth checking whether it's one production or two, because if you want to use either review in class, you'll want to know which show your pupils are reading about.

I should be honest that I only have the headlines and short summaries, not the full reviews. But even from those, there's a lovely teaching idea. "Infinite jest" is Hamlet's phrase, from the graveyard, when he holds Yorick's skull and remembers a man of infinite jest, most excellent fancy. A production that reaches for jest and childhood objects is, in a way, answering that line. Pupils in première might enjoy the question of what happens to a tragedy when you play it with playfulness, even toys. Does it dilute the grief, or does it sharpen it, by setting innocence beside death? Hamlet himself, after all, puts on an antic disposition, so comedy is already inside the play. You could give your pupils the two headlines with no further information and ask them to predict what the production is doing and why, then read the reviews together and see whether the critics found the gamble worthwhile. That tests prediction, inference and critical vocabulary all at once, and it's a gentle way into the idea that a text on the syllabus is a living thing that directors keep arguing with.

A third Hamlet is on screen rather than stage. The Hindu has published a review of a new Hamlet film starring Riz Ahmed, under the headline that he finds method in this madness. That wordplay, of course, nods to Polonius, who remarks that though this be madness, yet there is method in it. Again, I only have the headline and a short summary, so I can't tell you how the film is set or how it treats the text. What I can say is that it gives you a useful comparison. A stage production with soft toys on one side, a film with a leading actor on the other: two very different answers to the same question of how to make a four-hundred-year-old play speak now. For première pupils working on the madness, real or feigned, that headline alone could start a discussion. Is Hamlet mad, pretending, or something in between, and what does an actor have to decide in order to play him?

Two more Hamlet items are rather thinner. The University of Utah has published a piece asking why Hamlet still matters. All I have is that question, but it's a very good question to hand to a class. Before reading anything, you might ask pupils to write their own answer in three sentences, and then, if you track the article down, compare. For terminale, thinking ahead, it's the kind of prompt that trains a pupil to defend a view with evidence from the text rather than simply asserting that Shakespeare is timeless. Then BroadwayWorld has a video preview of Hamlet at the Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey, though the text is only a caption. A preview clip is short, and short clips are valuable in a lesson. If it turns out to include a few lines of the verse, you could use it to look at how an actor handles the soliloquy rhythm, where to breathe, which word to lean on. I can't promise that's what the clip contains, so do watch it first.

The last Hamlet item is the oddest, and perhaps the most fun. Starburst Magazine has an interview with Dan Sturman and R.C. Staab about Space Hamlet, a science-fiction reworking of Shakespeare's play. The extract is thin, so I can't tell you how much of the original survives in the retelling. But the idea alone is useful. Pupils often feel that Shakespeare belongs to a museum, and a reimagining that sends the Prince of Denmark into space says the opposite. You might ask: what would you have to keep for it still to be Hamlet? The ghost, the revenge, the doubt, the court that watches everyone? That question gets pupils to name what they think the play is really about, which is half the work of an essay.

Moving to Twelfth Night, also on the 2027 programme, there are two small items. Shakespeare's Globe has an official trailer for its production of the play, listed on IMDb. The summary gives nothing beyond the trailer itself, so I can't describe the casting or the staging. But a trailer from the Globe is a handy classroom taster, a minute or two to show seconde pupils before they open the text, to give them a sense of the colour, the music and the comedy. If the trailer shows the cross-dressing and the confusion, you have an easy bridge into the question of how Viola's disguise drives the plot. Do preview it, of course, since I can't vouch for what it shows.

The second Twelfth Night item comes from BroadwayWorld, which announces that Ellyn Heald's Twelfth Night: 1941 will have its world premiere at the Episcopal Actors' Guild in New York. The notice gives no date, so the only thing certain is the place. The title suggests that the play has been moved to a particular year, but I don't have details of how, so I'd treat that as an intriguing hint and nothing more. Still, the notion of relocating the comedy to a specific moment in history is a good prompt for pupils. What does a change of setting do to a play about disguise, longing and mistaken identity? Does a particular year make the festive mood feel more fragile, or more precious? Even without the details, it invites the question of what a director gains by choosing a time and place.

On to Friel. The Mount Temple Drama Group, in Westmeath in Ireland, is staging Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa, which is on the 2027 list. The item is brief, and I have no dates or cast. But it's a pleasing reminder that this play is performed by community and school groups as well as professional companies, and that there's a living tradition of staging it. For your pupils, Dancing at Lughnasa is a play about memory, told by a narrator looking back, and I know you love a strong narrator. Michael's voice, speaking from the present about a summer long ago, is a lovely way to talk about how a play can have a narrator at all, and how the dance, that wild moment when the sisters move to the music, works as language without words. If you're able to find photographs or a clip of the Westmeath production, it could help pupils picture how a local company handles that scene. As ever, it's worth checking that something is available before you promise it to a class.

Now, a novel rather than a play, and one I think you'll like. The Irish Times reviews Catherine Cliff's debut, Miss Bates: Emma Revisited, which retells Austen's Emma from the point of view of Miss Bates, the talkative, gossipy, overlooked woman of Highbury. The reviewer calls it witty and ambitious. Emma is on your oral themes list, so this is directly useful. It's a good example of what happens when a minor character is given the narrative. In Austen, Miss Bates is chiefly a source of comic chatter, and Emma's cruel remark to her at Box Hill is a turning point in the book. Giving her the voice invites pupils to reread that moment and ask what we miss when we only see someone through another character's eyes. It also touches the larger question of who gets to tell the story, which links neatly to your interest in narrators. For an oral, a pupil who can say something thoughtful about point of view in Emma, and who knows that a writer has taken the same book from the other side, has something distinctive to offer. I only have the review summary, so I can't tell you how the book handles the plot, but the premise is enough to start a good lesson.

Turning to the oral list's authors, there's a Financial Times essay on Cormac McCarthy, titled A Legacy Revisited, about the making of a myth. The extract is thin, so I can't summarise the argument. But the subject bears on The Road. The idea that a writer's reputation hardens into legend is a useful critical frame: pupils might ask how much of our reading of The Road is shaped by what we've heard about its author, and how much comes from the sparse, grave sentences on the page. It's a good question to ask before a close reading of a short passage, where the language can speak for itself.

Margaret Atwood appears twice. The Toronto Star reports that she has thousands of microplastics in her blood and is not happy about it. I have only the headline, so I'll leave it there. It's not a classroom text, but it shows Atwood, author of The Handmaid's Tale, still speaking publicly about the world, which pupils sometimes forget. The other mention is a festival announcement: the Miami Book Fair returns from the fifteenth to the twenty-second of November, with Atwood on the line-up, alongside Colson Whitehead, Tony Shalhoub and Bonnie Garmus. The National Law Review carries the notice. It's mainly useful as a sign that authors on your oral list are still appearing in public. If a recording or an interview comes out of her appearance, it could be useful for terminale, but nothing of that kind has been announced in what I have.

Finally, two items for the musical side of your life. AnOther Magazine has an Obsessions Index feature with the composer Max Richter. I only have the title, so I can't say what he's obsessed with, but if you enjoy a composer talking about what shapes his work, it may be worth a look. And Bloomberg reports that one of classical music's biggest stars says AI is degrading our taste. The text is brief, and I don't have the performer's name. It raises a question that sits comfortably alongside the teaching of literature: what happens to our sense of beauty when machines can produce something that sounds right? Your pupils may have views on that for writing as well as music.

That's the lot, Yamuna. Plenty of Hamlet to think about, and I hope something here makes it into your next lesson with a cup of tea beside it.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. This week's good news has a lot to do with things being saved, whether books, birds, or people's dignity, so let me start with the stories and the images.

Upworthy retells the story of H. A. and Margret Rey, the couple who created Curious George. During the Second World War they escaped the Nazis by bicycle, carrying their original manuscripts with them. It's a lovely piece of survival through literature, and it ends on a hopeful note. Something about the image of two people pedalling away from catastrophe with a monkey's adventures in their luggage is hard to forget. Also from Upworthy, a short piece on a detail that van Gogh hid in his painting "Café Terrace at Night", which went unnoticed for a century. The text is brief and I can't tell you from it exactly what the detail is, but it may be worth a look for your classes, as a reminder that a painting can keep a secret for a hundred years.

Staying with books, Beaux Arts Magazine reports that an anonymous benefactor has apparently rescued the cabinet des livres at the Château de Chantilly, a library of about thirteen thousand precious volumes. The article is cut off, so the details are thin, but the heart of it is clear: a mysterious donor, and a library kept safe for future readers. And on the history side, Good News Network notes that today is eight hundred and nine years since King Henry the Third signed the Charter of the Forest in England. It gave free men the right to use forests that had once been reserved for the crown. It makes a good companion to the Magna Carta story, and a reminder that rights can be as practical as the right to gather wood.

There's a thriller-ish note too. Scientists have finally cracked a puzzle that has lasted more than twenty years, according to Good News Network. A four-hundred-year-old padlock was found in a treasure-laden shipwreck on a Welsh beach, and the team used an ordinary hospital CT scanner to read its inner workings. And from the other side of the Atlantic, The Guardian features "Remember Me", opening today at the National Gallery of Art in Washington and running until the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. It brings together seventy early portrait photographs, showing how African Americans used the form to picture themselves and their communities. The Guardian has a gallery of images from it, and it's a strong example of pictures that carry history.

Now to nature, where the news is unusually concrete. Good News Network reports that sandwich terns have returned to a colony on England's south coast, three years after avian flu wiped it out. The numbers have gone from zero to seven hundred and fifty-six birds. Conservation work also helped little terns, ringed plovers, gulls and oystercatchers to recover. Far away, on the Indonesian island of Bangka, the Bangka slow loris, a venomous primate feared extinct for a hundred years, is still with us. A local wildlife group on the island rescues animals and returns them to the wild, which is conservation working at the level of ordinary, patient people.

There's a charming accident in a laboratory, too. The Optimist Daily carries a podcast from a Stanford lab describing how two coral fragments accidentally touched in a tank, and then began absorbing healthy algae through the point of contact. The researchers hadn't planned it, so it may hint at a way that bleached coral could recover. The episode also covers nine more solutions to other problems, if you want a longer listen. And there's a story about land: donors from around the world have raised millions to buy an estate that a British noble family held for eight hundred years. It's home to curlew, lapwing and mountain bumblebees, and it will now be protected for wildlife. That article is cut off, so I can't say more about the estate itself, but the idea of strangers pooling money to protect a landscape is a nice one.

And finally, people. Reasons to be Cheerful visits Erik's Ranch and Retreats, near Livingston, Montana, a guest retreat on two hundred and thirty acres of pasture and wilderness. There, autistic people work as concierges, guides, wranglers and cooks, and the whole place is built around its staff rather than asking them to fit in. In southern Brazil, Good News Network tells of Pedro Moro, who found a wad of cash in a public square and spent twelve days tracking down its owner. It turned out to be a young construction worker's entire monthly salary, withdrawn to pay for his daughter's needs. Twelve days is a long time to keep knocking on doors for a stranger.

From Upworthy comes the story of Eric Schultz, a Hawaiian teenager who spent years in homeless shelters and in his car, and who has now graduated from Waianae High School. Perseverance is an overused word, but here it fits.

Two last stories feel close to home. ARTE Regards has a thirty-minute reportage, available until twenty thirty-one, on a seniors' centre in Trastevere, in Rome. It serves more than two thousand retirees with painting and dance classes, shared meals and a good deal of solidarity. It's in French, and it sounds like a warm half-hour. And closer to Les Adrets, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on volunteers in Chambéry who are restoring old trains and putting them back on the rails. It's local heritage in the most literal sense, kept alive by people who simply think it's worth doing.

That's the news for today, and I hope some of it follows you out into the mountain air.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. The last two days have brought a lovely mix of stories, from books carried to safety and a padlock that kept its secret for four centuries, to birds coming back from the brink and a few quiet acts of decency, so let me take you through them.

I'll begin with books and the people who protect them, since that's where several of today's stories sit. Upworthy tells the story of H. A. and Margret Rey, the couple behind Curious George. During the Second World War they escaped the Nazis by bicycle, carrying their original manuscripts with them. It's a wonderful image: two people fleeing, with everything they could not bear to lose strapped to their bikes, and what they saved was a mischievous little monkey who has delighted children ever since. The piece calls it a human history of survival through literature, and it ends on a positive note. It's the sort of story that makes a good small opening to a lesson on why stories matter, and what people will risk to keep them.

On the subject of books saved, there is heartening news from France. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that a mysterious, anonymous benefactor has rescued the cabinet des livres at the Château de Chantilly. That is the library room of the château, which holds about thirteen thousand precious volumes. The report I have is cut short, so I can't tell you the details of the gift, but the headline itself is lovely: someone, who doesn't want any credit, has made sure that a great collection of books will be there for future readers.

There's also a story with the pull of a good thriller. Good News Network reports that scientists have finally cracked a puzzle that had lasted more than twenty years. A padlock, around four hundred years old, was found in a treasure-laden shipwreck on a Welsh beach. Nobody could open it or read it without damaging it, so the researchers took it to a hospital and used a CT scanner to look inside. After two decades of mystery, the puzzle is solved. There is something very satisfying about the idea that the same machine that helps doctors see inside a patient has now let us see inside a lock made before the modern age. It's a lovely little detective story, with an old object, a long wait, and a clever, unexpected tool.

From locks to paintings. Upworthy has a short piece about a detail that Vincent van Gogh hid in his painting Café Terrace at Night, one that went unnoticed for a hundred years. The piece is brief, so I can't tell you more than that, but the idea alone is a pleasure. A painting you may have looked at a hundred times, with its yellow light spilling onto the cobbles and the deep blue of the night sky, turns out still to have something left to reveal. It makes me think of how a novel or a poem can do the same thing, and how a reader can come back to a page and find something that was always there. If you're looking for a bridge between painting and text for your students, this might be a charming one.

Staying with images that carry history, The Guardian has a photo gallery about early Black portrait photography, under the title Identity, resilience and community. It accompanies an exhibition called Remember Me, which runs from the seventh of November to the fourteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven, at the National Gallery of Art in Washington. It brings together seventy works that show how African Americans used portrait photography to depict themselves and their own communities. The word "themselves" matters here. These are pictures made as acts of self-definition, on the sitters' own terms, and the Guardian's selection shows faces and clothes and poses chosen with great care. It is a fine example of how a single image can hold a whole history, and I suspect it would pair beautifully with a text in class.

And there's one more piece of history, this time about words rather than pictures. Good News Network's history column marks eight hundred and nine years since King Henry the Third signed the Charter of the Forest in England. It was a law that gave free men the right to use forests that had previously been reserved for the crown. The piece suggests reading it alongside the story of Magna Carta, and I like that. We tend to remember the grand charter and forget its humbler companion, which dealt with everyday rights: the woods, the places people relied on. It's a good reminder that liberty is often made of small, practical things.

Now to the natural world, where the news is unusually good. Good News Network reports a miracle recovery among seabirds in England. Avian flu wiped out a colony of Sandwich terns on the south coast. Three years later, the birds have come back, rising from zero to seven hundred and fifty-six. Conservation work has also helped little terns, ringed plovers, gulls and oystercatchers recover. Going from an empty beach to hundreds of birds is a tremendous change, and it shows that when people look after a place carefully, nature can respond more quickly than we dare hope.

There's another return, and this one is a little more exotic. The Bangka slow loris, a venomous primate that was feared to have been extinct for a hundred years, turns out to have been hiding in plain sight all along. Good News Network says it survives thanks to a local wildlife group on Bangka island, which rescues animals and returns them to the wild. What I like here is that the hope comes from people on the ground, close to the animals, rather than from some grand international plan. It's conservation at the scale of a small team doing patient, practical work.

Also on the conservation front, donors from around the world have raised millions to buy an estate that a British noble family held for eight hundred years. Good News Network reports that it is home to curlew, lapwing and mountain bumblebees, and that it will now be protected for wildlife. The article I have is cut off, so I can't give you the name of the estate or the wider details. But the shape of the story is clear and rather moving: eight centuries in one family's hands, and now a place held in trust, thanks to many strangers, for the birds and the bees.

And then there is a story from under the sea, which comes from The Optimist Daily's podcast. A Stanford lab was keeping coral in tanks, and two coral fragments happened to touch. Where they touched, one began absorbing healthy algae from the other. The researchers hadn't planned this, and it might point to a possible way that bleached coral can recover. Bleached coral has lost the algae that it lives with, so seeing a healthy partner passed along through simple contact is a hopeful sign. It's an accident that may turn into a discovery, and the podcast describes it as a story of healing. The episode also covers nine more solutions, if you fancy a longer listen.

Now to the people stories, which are all about dignity and decency, and I find them the warmest of all.

In Montana, near Livingston, Reasons to be Cheerful describes Erik's Ranch and Retreats. It's a guest retreat on two hundred and thirty acres of pasture and wilderness, where autistic people work as concierges, guides, wranglers and cooks. The story is about a place built around its staff, with the work shaped to suit the people doing it, rather than people being squeezed into a job that doesn't fit. It's a warm account of work and dignity, and of what happens when a workplace starts from the strengths of the people in it.

In southern Brazil, a man named Pedro Moro found a wad of cash in a public square. He could have kept it, but instead he spent twelve days tracking down its owner. Good News Network says it turned out to be a young construction worker's entire monthly salary, withdrawn to pay for his daughter's needs. Twelve days is a long time to keep looking, and it's the persistence that moves me. It wasn't a quick gesture but a decision he renewed each day until the money was back where it belonged. A quiet, humane story, and a lovely reminder of ordinary decency.

From Hawaii, Upworthy brings us the story of Eric Schultz, a teenager who spent years living in homeless shelters and in his car. He has now graduated from Waianae High School. The piece is about perseverance, and I'd add only that finishing school while your home keeps changing is an achievement far beyond the diploma itself. Congratulations to him.

Now a recommendation for an evening in, and one that I think suits your love of dance. ARTE Regards has a thirty-minute reportage titled Rome: retraités, mais toujours actifs, available until twenty thirty-one. It takes us to a seniors' centre in Trastevere, which serves more than two thousand retirees with painting classes, dance classes, shared meals and a strong spirit of solidarity. It sounds like the opposite of the lonely retirement we often hear about, with people painting, dancing and eating together in one of the most beautiful quarters of Rome. And since it's available for years to come, there's no rush.

Finally, something close to home. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports from Chambéry, where volunteers are restoring old trains and putting them back on the rails. It's a local heritage story with a clear sense of people doing something worthwhile together, spending their time to bring old machines back to life. It's not far from Les Adrets, so you may even be able to see the results for yourself one day, and I'd imagine it makes a pleasant outing, perhaps with a stop at a producers' market on the way.

Taken together, today's stories share a thread: someone, somewhere, took the trouble to keep something safe, whether it was a manuscript, a library, a forest law, a tern colony or a month's wages. I hope that gives you something to smile about over your coffee, and have a lovely Saturday.
