Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the seventh of November, and this week's France news has trains arriving, schools under strain, and a good deal for a lover of words to enjoy.

Let me begin with the good news, which is on the rails. On Friday, the first six of SNCF's new TGV M trains entered service. The Local France has been looking inside them, and the headline features are a bar carriage, spaces for bicycles, a holder for your phone, and better accessibility for passengers in wheelchairs. Franceinfo, meanwhile, followed the new-generation TGV Inoui on its first commercial run, between Paris and Marseille. It arrives almost two years behind schedule, and one of the people quoted says, in effect, that the difficulties have been overcome and they now have a very good train. The promises are more legroom, new bar carriages and generally greater comfort. If you're planning any journeys south this winter, it's worth knowing these trains are beginning to appear, though I'd not assume you'll find one on your particular route just yet.

Now to schools, where the mood is rather more sober. Franceinfo reports that around thirty head teachers from Paris gathered outside the Sorbonne on Thursday to speak up for their profession. They describe working under constant strain and facing violence of what they call an unprecedented gravity. One of them put it this way: whatever we do, we are caught in a vice. Another warned of a situation that can explode on a daily basis. All of this is set against the backdrop of continuing protests by lycée students, which are putting pressure on schools across the country.

On a related note, and a much more concrete one, franceinfo also reports on an incident in Lyon. On Friday morning, rubbish bins were set alight in front of the Édouard-Herriot lycée, and the fire spread to the main door of the building. Pupils were evacuated. It's the kind of story that will feel close to home for anyone who works in a lycée, even in a different city, so I'll simply say that it's a reminder of why those head teachers are speaking out.

There's also a video from HugoDécrypte, the channel that explains the day's news in a clear, calm way. Its subject is the government's list of ten lycées that are to be renovated urgently. I can't tell you from the description which schools are on the list, so I don't know whether any are in the Grenoble area or the wider region. But as someone who teaches in a lycée, you might find it interesting to watch and see whether the conditions described resemble anything you know from your own school.

And one more piece of education news, this time about the road to university. Franceinfo looks at the announced end of Parcoursup, the national platform through which French students apply to higher education. Its disappearance has revived an old and thorny debate. On one side is what the piece calls an openly acknowledged selection of students by universities. On the other is the idea of no sorting at all. The question is becoming more urgent because the number of baccalauréat holders keeps rising. For your première pupils and those you'll be teaching in terminale, this is useful background, since it's the system they will be stepping into, and the debate about how fair it is will likely continue for some time.

Let's turn to something gentler, and to your own territory: language. The Local France has several short pieces this week that are a pleasure for anyone who loves French and its oddities. The first is the weekly La Belle Vie column, which this time explores some of the quirks of the French language alongside a declared love of cheese. The text is brief, but it's a light and cheerful read, and given where you live, with the markets of the Grésivaudan not far away, the cheese part may feel quite personal.

The same publication has a piece on what are called gentilés, the names given to the people who live in French towns. Some of them, apparently, are surprisingly hard to guess. It's a small, pleasant piece of linguistic local colour, and I suspect it might make a nice warm-up exercise for a class, if you ever wanted to see how your pupils fare with the inhabitants of unfamiliar towns.

Then there's the French Word of the Day, which is "charrier". The Local presents it as a jovial word, one that shouldn't be taken too seriously, which is rather a nice thing to say about a word. And the French Expression of the Day is "troisième tour dans la rue", literally a third round in the street. The piece links it to the coming presidential election. It's short, but idioms like this are always delightful to collect, since they tell you so much about how a language thinks about public life.

From idiom to literature. This is the story I most wanted to save for you. The novelist Philippe Jaenada, who won the Goncourt, has written a letter to the news agency AFP defending his use of artificial intelligence in his novel L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. He describes that use as "amusée" and "ironique", amused and ironic, and he insists it was limited. Among the things he mentions is that he hid a sentence of ten words in the book. The debate sits at a fascinating crossing of questions: what counts as authorship, what a narrator's voice really is, and whether playing with a machine can itself be a literary gesture. I only have the outline from franceinfo, so I can't tell you more about how the passage works in the novel. But as a starting point for a conversation with older pupils about voice, originality and technology, it's a lively one. I'd also say that Jaenada's tone, playful and a little wry, seems very much in keeping with the kind of narrator you tend to enjoy.

Now a little history. The Guardian has published an archive piece looking back at how the paper itself reported the Suez crisis of 1956. That was when Nasser nationalised the canal, and Britain, France and Israel attacked. Looking back, the piece judges the paper's coverage as wrong on almost every count, and the title says as much: wrong on every count. What I like about it is that it gives you history through contemporary writing, the voice of the moment rather than the summary of historians afterwards. Since you often find that texts teach the past better than textbooks, this might be a lovely thing to read slowly, perhaps with a view to how journalism, like fiction, shapes our sense of what happened. It also has an obvious link to the shared Anglo-French story, since France was one of the three countries involved.

And on the subject of history and fiction, The Local France has an analysis asking why there are so many films set during the Second World War in French cinemas right now. Several of the most successful French films of 2026 are set in that period, and the piece asks whether this says something about modern anxieties. It's mostly angled at the box office and the film industry, which I know is not your priority, so I'll leave it there. But the underlying question, why do we keep returning to the same years, and what do stories about the past tell us about the present, is one that a literature teacher might well find rewarding.

Now the weather, or rather the climate, and I'm afraid this isn't cheerful. Franceinfo reports that the Copernicus climate service has found that October 2026 was the hottest October ever recorded. It points to record heat at the surface of the oceans, linked to El Niño. Copernicus adds that 2026 will probably be the second-hottest year on record. It's a sober piece of news rather than a surprise, but I think it's right to mention it, especially for those of us who live in the mountains and watch the seasons closely.

Finally, the daily video from La Mire, the programme that gathers up the oddities of French television. The edition from the fifth of November was dominated by coverage of the American election and the war in Iran, with one line quoted from the episode's title referring to twelve billion dollars in advertising. Heavy material, then, but the programme has its lighter moments. The most appealing segments are Keren Ann's cover of Dolly Parton's "Jolene", which is a lovely thing to be reminded of, a French-based singer taking on one of the great narrators of heartbreak in song. There's also a light item about a platypus fight, which I'll let you discover for yourself.

That's the picture from France this morning. Do enjoy your Saturday, and perhaps treat yourself to a good piece of cheese at the market.

Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Saturday. Here is your Daily Yam for the seventh of November.

Let me begin with paintings, since two good stories come from Hyperallergic. In the first, Catherine Ostler follows the two girls in Renoir's "Pink and Blue". They grew up in a privileged, elite, artistic French family, and their lives were overturned by the Holocaust. It's a story that begins with a canvas of two sweet-faced sisters and leads somewhere much darker, which is just the sort of thing you like to set beside a novel. The second comes from Boston. The Museum of Fine Arts is setting up a pop-up restoration studio where visitors can watch live conservation of a seventeenth-century group portrait of an Amsterdam wine guild, by Nicolaes Eliasz Pickenoy. It's a rare chance to see a painting being brought back to life, one careful stroke at a time.

On to books, and a rich morning for them. The Guardian has gathered this year's Booker finalists, among them Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout, to describe where their novels began. The hints are delicious: a trip to the Scottish islands, a psychological experiment, and a chance encounter in a drugstore. Small sparks, apparently, for large books. Meanwhile, the Booker Prizes site offers two treats of its own. One is an extract from Max Porter's "Lanny", which gives you a direct taste of that novel's voice and language, and is well worth reading aloud to yourself with a coffee. The other is a list of eight prize-winning novels inspired by folklore, tracing the line from fiction back to myth and older traditions of storytelling.

And for the teaching side of your week, two pieces for the BFI corner. The Observer reviews "The Last Hamlet" by the company Lost Dog, a production that mixes Shakespeare with soft toys and what the paper calls shambolic charm. It's a fresh theatrical angle on a play that's on the twenty twenty-seven programme, so it might spark an idea for your terminale classes. The Irish Times, meanwhile, reviews Catherine Cliff's debut, "Miss Bates: Emma Revisited", which retells Austen's "Emma" through the gossipy, overlooked Miss Bates. The reviewer calls it witty and ambitious. Since "Emma" is on the oral themes list, it could offer students a new way in: what changes when the chatterbox, rather than the heroine, holds the narrative?

Staying with books, but crossing into France, there's a lively literary quarrel. Philippe Jaenada, the Goncourt-winning novelist, has written to the news agency AFP to defend what he calls his "amused" and "ironic" use of artificial intelligence. He used it only in a limited way in "L'Inconnue du quai de Javel", and, in a nice touch, he hid a ten-word sentence in it. That's a debate your students might enjoy picking apart. And on a lighter linguistic note, The Local France has its French Word of the Day: "charrier". It's a jovial word, the piece says, and not one to be taken too seriously, so if someone tells you you're exaggerating, you might just be told that you're "charriant".

Now, something to watch. ARTE Concert has a documentary on Klaus Nomi, the German-born countertenor of cold wave, an early queer icon who died of AIDS in nineteen eighty-three. It's described as stylised and moving, and sounds like a portrait you'd enjoy: a strange, singular voice and a character who stepped out of nowhere. And if you prefer dance, The Times has an interview marking twenty-five years of BalletBoyz. The founders look back on a quarter of a century, and on the name they say they never liked. It's a warm, character-led read for a Saturday.

Now for some good news. Donors from around the world have raised millions to buy an estate that a British noble family held for eight hundred years. It's home to curlew, lapwing and mountain bumblebees, and it will now be protected for wildlife conservation. The article I saw was cut off, so I can't tell you more of the detail, but the headline alone is cheering. And from Bangka island comes the story of the Bangka slow loris, a venomous primate once feared extinct. It survives, it turns out, thanks to a local wildlife group that rescues animals and returns them to the wild. It's a hopeful account of conservation working on the ground, by people who simply got on with it.

Finally, closer to home. This evening, from half past six until ten, the village hall in Saint-Jean-le-Vieux hosts an evening of Belledonne-themed storytelling and gatherings, part of the Grésivaudan agenda. For someone who loves narrators and local life, it sounds like a very good Saturday night, and not far from Les Adrets. And in Chambéry, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells of volunteers who are restoring old trains and putting them back on the rails. It's a warm heritage story about people doing something worthwhile, with their own hands.

That's the Daily Yam for today, Yamuna. I hope your Saturday is full of good stories, whether you read them or hear them told by the fire.
